Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Vignette:
Thomas, a 45-year-old military medic, found himself deployed to a remote region in the aftermath of a devastating earthquake. The initial tremor had been terrifying, but it was the days and weeks that followed that truly fractured his world. He remembered the constant, low rumble of aftershocks, the deafening roar of structures collapsing around him as he worked, and the desperate cries of the injured echoing through the dust-filled air. He’d been trying to extract a trapped child when a secondary collapse had sent a torrent of debris cascading down, nearly burying him alive. The sound of splintering wood and crumbling concrete had been overwhelming, a moment frozen in time.

Now, months later, when Thomas tried to recount those events, he found himself lost in a jumble of fragmented images and raw sensations. He couldn't put the memories of the event in the right order; one moment he was seeing a child's face, the next he was back under the dust cloud, then hearing a distant siren, all out of sequence. When the memory returned, it brought back the same terror he felt at the time, his heart hammering against his ribs, his breath catching in his throat. He would often feel so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, needing several minutes to compose himself before he could even attempt to speak again.

Back on base, and later in his quiet apartment, Thomas found himself constantly on edge. He was on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds. The sudden slam of a door, a car backfiring outside, or even a dropped tray in the mess hall would make him jump and send a surge of adrenaline through him. His body would tense, and his eyes would dart around, scanning for any potential threat. He was superalert or watchful or on guard all the time, a state of hypervigilance that never seemed to abate. He’d try to relax in the evenings, perhaps watch a movie, but his mind would still be monitoring every creak of the building, every distant siren, every rustle outside his window. He was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, the constant internal tension a heavy burden.

Before the earthquake, Thomas had been a man of purpose, proud of his service and his ability to help others. He had believed in a certain order to the world, in the resilience of communities, and in the inherent goodness of people. But the sheer scale of the destruction and suffering he witnessed, the random cruelty of the disaster, had completely destroyed his beliefs about how the world works. He felt like he didn't know himself anymore; the confident, capable medic he once was seemed to have vanished, replaced by a stranger constantly gripped by anxiety. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore, not his deployments, not the camaraderie of his unit, not even the quiet solitude he once cherished. His late wife, who had passed a few years prior, felt even further away now, her memory clouded by this new, pervasive emptiness.

His hypervigilance and inability to relax had started to affect his work at the base clinic. He found it difficult to concentrate on patient charts, his attention constantly pulled away by the sounds of the bustling clinic. He’d often snap at colleagues over minor issues, feeling perpetually irritable. He had also begun to isolate himself, avoiding social gatherings and even the mess hall during peak hours, preferring to eat alone in his apartment to avoid the unpredictable sounds and movements of others. This withdrawal had not gone unnoticed, and his commanding officer had recently called him in, expressing concern about his performance and his increasingly distant demeanor. It was this conversation, coupled with a deep, aching weariness, that finally prompted Thomas to seek help. He desperately wanted to find his way back to himself, but what frightened him most was the persistent dread that the meaningful life he once knew was gone forever.
